questions.problem:
The velocity $v$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
v(t)=⟨t(6t-4),\,12{t}^{3}⟩.
$$

Given that the particle is at the position $(20,30)$ when $t=2,$ calculate the components of the position vector of $P$ at time $t.$

$r(t)=⟨${{field-1}}$,\,3{t}^{4}-18\,⟩$
questions.worked_solution:
To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨t(6t-4),\,12{t}^{3}⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int t(6t-4)\,\text{d}t,\,\int 12{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨2{t}^{3}-2{t}^{2}+{C}_{1},\,3{t}^{4}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(2)=⟨20,30⟩.$ Substituting $t=2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(2) & =⟨2(2)^{3}-2(2)^{2}+{C}_{1},\,3(2)^{4}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨20,30⟩ & =⟨8+{C}_{1},48+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=12$ and ${C}_{2}=-18.$ Therefore, the position vector is

$$
r(t)=⟨2{t}^{3}-2{t}^{2}+12,\,3{t}^{4}-18⟩.
$$

$$
v=⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{t+1}},\,-1⟩,\,t\ge 0.

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{t+1}},\,-1⟩\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{t+1}}\,\text{d}t,\,\int (-1)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨2\sqrt{t+1}+{C}_{1},\,-t+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(3) & =⟨2\sqrt{3+1}+{C}_{1},\,-3+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨5,2⟩ & =⟨4+{C}_{1},-3+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=1$ and ${C}_{2}=5.$ Therefore, the position vector is

$$
r(t)=⟨2\sqrt{t+1}+1,\,5-t⟩.
$$

$$
v=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩.

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t,\,\int \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{C}_{1},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(\frac{\pi }{2})=⟨0,0⟩.$ Substituting $t=\frac{\pi }{2},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+{C}_{1},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨0,0⟩ & =⟨{C}_{1},1+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}

so we must have ${C}_{1}=0$ and ${C}_{2}=-1.$ Therefore, the position vector is

$$
r(t)=⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t-1⟩.

To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨6t-1,{t}^{2}-1⟩\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int (6t-1)\,\text{d}t,\int ({t}^{2}-1)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨3{t}^{2}-t+{C}_{1},\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}-t+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(3)=⟨10,-1⟩.$ Substituting $t=3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(3) & =⟨3({3}^{2})-3+{C}_{1},\frac{{3}^{3}}{3}-3+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨10,-1⟩ & =⟨24+{C}_{1},6+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=-14$ and ${C}_{2}=-7.$ Therefore, the position vector at time $t$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨3{t}^{2}-t-14,\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}-t-7⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =⟨3({1}^{2})-1-14,\frac{{1}^{3}}{3}-1-7⟩ \\  & =⟨-12,-\frac{23}{3}⟩.\end{aligned}

so we must have ${C}_{1}=1$ and ${C}_{2}=2.$ Therefore, the position vector at time $t$ is given by

$$
v(t)=⟨\frac{2}{t+1},\,2t-5⟩,\,t\in (0,\infty ).
$$

Given that the particle is at the position $r=⟨0,6⟩$ when $t=0,$ find the times when the particle intersects the $x$-axis. Do not round the answers.

In **ascending order**, the particle intersects the $x$-axis when $t=$
{{field-1}}

{{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
The particle intersects the $x$-axis when its position is $r=⟨x,0⟩,$ where $x$ is arbitrary. So first, we need to compute the position function of the particle.

To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨\frac{2}{t+1},\,2t-5⟩\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int \frac{2}{t+1}\,\text{d}t,\,\int (2t-5)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨2\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)+{C}_{1},\,{t}^{2}-5t+{C}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(0)=⟨0,6⟩.$ Substituting $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨2\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)+{C}_{1},\,{0}^{2}-5(0)+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨0,6⟩ & =⟨{C}_{1},\,{C}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we must have ${C}_{1}=0$ and ${C}_{2}=6.$ Therefore, the position of $P$ at time $t$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨2\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1),\,{t}^{2}-5t+6⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the times when the particle intersects the $x$-axis, we solve for the times at which the $y$-coordinate of the position vector is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}-5t+6 & =0 \\ (t-2)(t-3) & =0 \\ t & =2,\,3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, in ascending order, the particle intersects the $x$-axis when $t=2$ and $t=3.$

To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨2t-3,\,3{t}^{2}-6t+2⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int (2t-3)\,\text{d}t,\,\int (3{t}^{2}-6t+2)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{2}-3t+{C}_{1},\,{t}^{3}-3{t}^{2}+2t+{C}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨0-0+{C}_{1},\,0-0+0+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨2,0⟩ & =⟨{C}_{1},\,{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=2$ and ${C}_{2}=0.$ Therefore, the position of $P$ at time $t$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨{t}^{2}-3t+2,\,{t}^{3}-3{t}^{2}+2t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{t}^{2}-3t+2,\,{t}^{3}-3{t}^{2}+2t⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So we need

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}-3t+2 & =(t-1)(t-2)=0\,⇒\,t=1,2, \\ {t}^{3}-3{t}^{2}+2t & =t(t-1)(t-2)=0\,⇒\,t=0,1,2.\end{aligned}

The values of $t$ that satisfy both equations are $t=1$ and $t=2.$

We can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $\mathbf{v} (0)= \langle 2,\, 0 \rangle.$ Substituting $t=0,$ we get

\begin{aligned}v(0) & =⟨3\operatorname{sin}⁡0+{C}_{1},\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡0+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨2,\,0⟩ & =⟨{C}_{1},-1+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have $C_1=2$ and $C_2=1.$ Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
\mathbf{v}(t) = \left<      3\sin{3t} +2 , \,    1-\cos{t} \right>.
$$

We can compute the position vector by integrating the velocity vector.

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨3\operatorname{sin}⁡3t+2,\,1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 3\operatorname{sin}⁡3t+2\,\text{d}t,\,\int 1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡3t+2t+{C}_{3},\,t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{C}_{4}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $\mathbf{r} (0)= \langle 0,0 \rangle.$ Substituting $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡0+2(0)+{C}_{3},\,0-\operatorname{sin}⁡0+{C}_{4}⟩ \\ ⟨0,0⟩ & =⟨-1+{C}_{3},\,{C}_{4}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have $C_3=1$ and $C_4=0.$ Therefore, the position of $P$ at time $t$ is

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \left<  -\cos {3t} + 2t + 1 , \,   t-\sin{t}  \right>.
$$
